svg.title: VFR charts and ways around Class B
svg.desc: Which VFR chart to use: a sectional at 1 to 500,000 scale for cross-country planning and a Terminal Area Chart at 1 to 250,000 for the busy area around a Class B airport. A VFR flyway planning chart is a planning aid printed on the back of some Terminal Area Charts and suggests paths around Class B airspace. A VFR flyway is a general path, not an ATC route or clearance. A VFR corridor is a defined channel through Class B airspace.
svg.text: VFR charts and ways around Class B
Use the chart that fits the job, and check its effective date before every flight.
Sectional
1 : 500,000 (1 inch is about 6.9 NM)
Cross-country planning. Airports, airspace,
obstructions, navaids and terrain.
Terminal Area Chart (TAC)
1 : 250,000 (1 inch is about 3.4 NM)
Busy Class B areas. Twice the detail, so rings
and shelves are easier to read.
VFR Flyway Planning Chart
Printed on the back of some TACs. A planning aid that suggests paths around, under or near Class B.
It is not an ATC route and not a clearance.
Flyway: a general path around Class B
Class B, plan view
VFR flyway
A general flight path for planning
flights into, out of, through or near
complex terminal airspace, to avoid
Class B. No clearance is given; you
keep your own lookout and weather
minimums.
VFR corridor
A defined channel through Class B (a
"hole"); no clearance needed.
Source: Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; AIM ch. 3; 14 CFR 91.103. Read the chart legend and AIM for local rules.
